title: Would Meatball Survive? Pilot pack (10 Shorts)
_note: Series 'Would Meatball Survive?' (Showrunner, 2026-10-24). Shorts v2 (research/38, research/39 §6): frame 0 is a moving full-bleed photo with the claim stated as fact, a new picture every <=3 s (cuts on 'at' words), one Fork + one tink max per Short, verdict card ('Survival odds / Delicious odds') with a rotating third tag, loop line runs into the hook. 'shot' is the pending Studio shot grammar (host|show|closeup|together), ignored by the current renderer. 'sources' sits on each hook beat. SCRIPTS ONLY: do not render until the new Meatball rig is approved; the series takes the 1 PM YouTube Short slot after that (OPERATIONS.md, experiment E6). Photos: iNaturalist CC0/CC BY, looked at one by one (live, unharmed, right species, no watermark in crop). Moose 92166840/102548882 are 960 px with a bottom-left watermark: crops stop at y=0.9 and both are held under 3 s; swap if the render looks soft. Studio 10/24: voice set to Bill (OPERATIONS.md 'Narrator voice'); 5 of 10 Shorts (cassowary, moose, komodo, croc, boxjelly) end on a spoken comment question just before the loop line ('Always ask'), never in the first 3 s.

beats.say: A cassowary has a dagger on each foot. The inner toe ends in a claw up to four inches long.
beats.loop_say: Just so you know why I'm leaving early,
beats.short_title: A Cassowary Has a 4-Inch Dagger on Each Foot 🦶
beats.bonus: In 2019 a pet cassowary killed its owner in Florida after he fell near it.
beats.comment: Would you get within kicking distance of this bird? 👇
sources: San Diego Zoo, quoted in 2019 coverage: 'a dagger-like claw on the inner toe that is up to 4 inches (10 centimeters) long'; 'can slice open any predator or potential threat with a single swift kick' — https://bangordailynews.com/2019/04/15/news/nation/large-flightless-bird-kills-florida-man-in-horrible-accident/
Mental Floss, 10 facts about cassowaries (inner-toe claw ~5 in; fruit-eaters that swallow fruit whole and disperse the seeds) — https://www.mentalfloss.com/animals/birds/10-facts-about-cassowaries
Claw length: sources range 10-13 cm; script uses the conservative 'up to four inches'.

beats.say: One kick can slice open a threat.
Mostly, it eats fruit. It swallows the fruit whole.
Round. Whole. Bite-sized. I've been called all three.
Survival odds: zero. Delicious odds: high. Fruit odds: relevant.
Would you survive this? Comment.
Hippos can't actually swim. They're too heavy to float, so they bounce along the bottom.
beats.loop_say: So if the riverbed starts moving, that's why.
beats.bonus: A hippo can close its nostrils and ears underwater.
beats.comment: Did you know hippos can't float? 👇
sources: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, 'Making Waves' (hippos too dense to float; push off and walk the riverbed in a slow-motion gallop) — https://stories.sdzwa.org/?p=146524
Snopes, hippos are too dense to swim — https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/hippos-dense-swim/
San Diego Zoo animal profile (close nostrils, hold breath 5 min or longer) — https://animals.sandiegozoo.org/node/111
BBC Discover Wildlife (float up to breathe and sink back without waking) — https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/can-hippos-breathe-underwater
Hippos are herbivores (grazers): San Diego Zoo profile above.

beats.say: They hold their breath five minutes, and surface to breathe in their sleep.
Good news: they eat grass. Bad news: they're very grumpy about their river.
It wouldn't even eat me. Just flatten me. Worse.
Survival odds: low. Delicious odds: irrelevant. It's a furious vegetarian.
A moose can swim six miles an hour, for up to two hours. Rowing away is not a plan.
beats.loop_say: I asked about escaping by boat. The answer:
beats.short_title: A Moose Can Swim for Two Hours Straight 🫎
beats.bonus: Moose have been seen swimming more than ten miles to reach food.
beats.comment: Would you have guessed a moose could outswim you? 👇
sources: Alaska Dept. of Fish and Game, moose: swim at 6 mph for up to two hours — https://www.adfg.alaska.gov/index.cfm?adfg=viewing.landmammals&species=moose

Teton Science Schools, 'Can Moose Really Dive?' (moose readily submerge entirely to feed on aquatic plants; up to ~50 s underwater; swims of 10+ miles; the popular 18-20 ft depth figure is unproven, so the script gives no depth) — https://tetonscience.org/can-moose-really-dive/

beats.say: It even ducks right under water to eat plants off the bottom.
Big, grumpy, and a great swimmer. I can't swim at all.
Meatballs don't swim. We simmer.
Survival odds: low. Delicious odds: high. Swimming odds: please don't.
Could you outswim a moose? Comment.
This snail hunts fish with insulin. It clouds the water, and the fish's blood sugar crashes.
beats.loop_say: And you thought your snacks were weird.
beats.short_title: This Snail Hunts Fish With a Cloud of Insulin 🐚
beats.bonus: Scientists are studying cone snail insulin for faster-acting diabetes medicine.
beats.comment: Would you ever pick up a pretty shell again? 👇
sources: Safavi-Hemami et al. 2015, PNAS, 'Specialized insulin is used for chemical warfare by fish-hunting cone snails' (Conus geographus, C. tulipa) — https://archive.unews.utah.edu/news_releases/killer-snail-venom-insulin/
Cone snail harpoon = modified, barbed, hollow radular tooth fired from an extendable proboscis — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cone_snail
Conus geographus: about 36 recorded human deaths; no antivenom — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conus_geographus
Photo note: the harpoon beat uses Californiconus californicus (also a venomous cone snail, line is about cone snails in general); insulin and 'killed people' beats use C. geographus only.

beats.say: Then it fires a harpoon: a hollow, venom-filled tooth.
This one has killed people. There's no antivenom.
It swallows fish whole. I'm fish-sized. I'm walking faster.
Survival odds: high, actually. It's a snail. Just never pick one up.
Honey badgers are built to resist cobra venom. A tiny change in their muscles blocks part of the toxin.
beats.short_title: Honey Badgers Are Built to Resist Cobra Venom 🦡
beats.bonus: The same receptor change evolved separately in honey badgers, hedgehogs, pigs and mongooses.
beats.comment: Which animal would you least want to annoy? 👇
sources: Drabeck, Dean & Jansa 2015, Toxicon, 'Why the honey badger don't care: convergent evolution of venom-targeted nicotinic acetylcholine receptors' (honey badger, hedgehog, pig; mongoose known earlier) — https://experts.umn.edu/en/publications/why-the-honey-badger-dont-care-convergent-evolution-of-venom-targ/

Slate summary (receptor change blocks alpha-neurotoxin binding; resistance, not immunity) — https://www.slate.com/blogs/wild_things/2015/06/16/honey_badger_venom_resistance_biologists_discover_the_secret.html
Mental Floss summary (diet incl. snakes, scorpions, bee larvae) — https://www.mentalfloss.com/article/65209/science-confirms-honey-badger-dont-care
Wording rule: 'resist' / 'blocks part of', never 'immune'.

beats.say: Hedgehogs, mongooses and pigs evolved the same trick.
It eats almost anything. Snakes, scorpions, bee larvae.
Almost anything. I'll be very quiet now.
Survival odds: zero. Delicious odds: high. Its odds: doesn't care.
A Komodo dragon can eat eighty percent of its own weight in one meal. Its stomach just stretches.
beats.loop_say: So when someone says grab a bite, remember:
beats.short_title: A Komodo Dragon Can Eat 80% of Its Weight in One Meal 🦎
beats.bonus: Komodo dragons can go weeks without eating between big meals.
beats.comment: What's the most you've ever eaten in one sitting? 👇
sources: Smithsonian's National Zoo, Komodo dragon: stomach expands so an adult can consume up to 80% of its body weight in a single meal — https://www.nationalzoo.si.edu/node/6852
Cincinnati Zoo (same 80% figure) — https://cincinnatizoo.org/animals-archive/komodo-dragon/
Fry et al. 2009, PNAS (venom glands in the lower jaw) — https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/venomous-komodo-dragons-kill-prey-with-wound-and-poison-tactics
Contested: the venom's role in kills (LITFL, 'Komodo dragons: myth vs reality') — https://litfl.com/komodo-dragons-myth-vs-reality/ ; the script says it is argued.

beats.say: It has venom glands in its jaw. How much they matter is still argued.
Eighty percent of a meatball is a meatball. I don't love it.
One gulp. No chewing. No dignity.
Survival odds: zero. Delicious odds: high. Leftovers: none.
Could you eat that much? Comment.
Piranhas don't group up to hunt. They group up because they're scared of being eaten.
beats.loop_say: Honestly? Relatable. Which is why I say,
beats.short_title: Piranhas Travel in Groups Because They're Scared 🐟
beats.bonus: Only a couple of the roughly 25 piranha species are known to bark.
beats.comment: Did movies ruin piranhas for you? 👇
sources: Queiroz & Magurran 2005, Biology Letters 1:155-157, 'Safety in numbers? Shoaling behaviour of the Amazonian red-bellied piranha' (higher opercular rate in small shoals; slower recovery after a model-cormorant attack) — https://research-portal.st-andrews.ac.uk/en/publications/safety-in-numbers-shoaling-behaviour-of-the-amazonian-red-bellied/
St Andrews release, 'Rehabilitating piranhas' (groups for protection, not pack hunting) — https://news.st-andrews.ac.uk/archive/rehabilitating-piranhas/
Millot, Vandewalle & Parmentier 2011, J. Exp. Biol. 214:3613 (bark when handled) — https://www.npr.org/sections/thetwo-way/2011/10/14/141350706/listen-up-heres-how-some-piranhas-bark-before-they-bite
Photo note: all piranha photos are live aquarium fish (iNat captive/casual); every wild research-grade CC photo showed a caught or dead fish.

beats.say: In a lab, small groups breathed faster, a stress sign, and calmed slower after a fake bird attack.
They even bark when they're grabbed.
Scared fish, sharp teeth. And I'm, technically, meat.
Survival odds: decent. Delicious odds: still high.
Saltwater crocodiles have the strongest bite ever measured. About thirty-seven hundred pounds of force.
beats.loop_say: Someone measured that with a bite sensor. Brave. Anyway,
beats.short_title: Saltwater Crocodiles Have the Strongest Bite Ever Measured 🐊
beats.bonus: The previous record holder was an American alligator.
sources: Erickson et al. 2012, PLOS ONE (all 23 living crocodilian species); FSU release: 3,700 lb of bite force, highest ever recorded — https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2012/03/120316093427.htm
Guinness World Records: 16,414 N (about 3,690 lbf) from a saltwater crocodile — https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/401566-strongest-molariform-bite-force-for-a-crocodile
Units: 'pounds of force', not 'psi' (Nat Geo's psi is a unit slip).
Crocodilians cannot chew; they tear and swallow chunks — https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/120315-crocodiles-bite-force-erickson-science-plos-one-strongest

beats.say: Scientists tested all twenty-three crocodile species. The saltwater croc won.
Crocodiles can't chew. They clamp, twist, and swallow chunks whole.
I'm already chunk-sized. No twist needed.
Survival odds: zero. Delicious odds: high. Bite odds: record.
Would you hold the sensor? Comment.
A blue-ringed octopus bite can be painless. You might not notice it. And there's no antivenom.
beats.loop_say: So the blue rings are a courtesy. Because
beats.short_title: A Blue-Ringed Octopus Bite Can Be Painless 🐙
beats.bonus: It's small enough to fit in your palm, which is exactly why you shouldn't pick one up.
beats.comment: Did you know the bite might not even hurt? 👇
sources: Divers Alert Network (bite usually painless or like a bee sting; tetrodotoxin paralysis incl. breathing; no antivenom; full recovery expected with timely ventilation and care) — https://dan.org/health-medicine/health-resources/diseases-conditions/blue-ringed-octopus/

SBS, surviving a blue-ringed octopus bite (no antivenom; treat like a snake bite) — https://www.sbs.com.au/language/italian/en/podcast-episode/ep-259-occhio-al-polpo-dagli-anelli-blu-affascinante-ma-velenoso/vh52lyas1
Rings flash when threatened; eats crabs and shrimp — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hapalochlaena

beats.say: Its venom stops your breathing muscles. People survive if someone breathes for them.
When it's upset, the blue rings get brighter.
It eats crabs. Not meatballs. I checked. From far away.
Survival odds: good, with a friend. Delicious odds: low, for once.
A box jellyfish has twenty-four eyes, and no brain. Four of its eyes always look up.
beats.loop_say: So it's watching you right now. Because
beats.short_title: A Box Jellyfish Has 24 Eyes and No Brain 👀
beats.bonus: In Australia, vinegar is the first aid for box jellyfish stings, then emergency help.
beats.comment: Twenty-four eyes and no brain. Who does that remind you of? 👇
sources: Garm et al. 2011, Current Biology (24 eyes of four types; upper and lower lens eyes form images; four always look up; used to navigate) — https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2011/04/110428123938.htm
Scientific American, 'Box Jellyfish Eyes Aim at the Trees' (no real brain; active hunters) — https://www.scientificamerican.com/podcast/episode/box-jellyfish-eyes-aim-at-the-trees-11-04-29/

Chironex fleckeri: unconsciousness and respiratory or cardiac arrest within minutes (Fenner 2005, Diving and Hyperbaric Medicine) — https://dhmjournal.com/images/IndividArticles/35June/Fenner_dhm.35.2.76-83.pdf

Photo note: no CC0/CC BY Chironex fleckeri photo exists on iNaturalist; photos are Carybdea xaymacana, Alatina alata and Copula sivickisi (all box jellyfish, all share the 24-eye layout). The Chironex line runs on a text card.

beats.say: Some of its eyes have lenses, like ours. It steers. It doesn't just drift.
In Australia, one kind can stop a human heart in minutes.
It eats small fish. No brain to add meatballs.
Survival odds: low. Delicious odds: unknown. It can't think about it.
Would you swim there? Comment.
